title: Numeric functions and calculations
summary_md: Rounding, truncation, modulo, integer vs decimal division, percentages, casting and GREATEST/LEAST, with the MySQL and SQL Server differences interviewers like.

sections.heading: ROUND(x, d)
sections.body_md:
- Position 1 = the number, position 2 = digits to keep. `d > 0` keeps decimals, `d = 0` rounds to a whole number, `d < 0` rounds to tens/hundreds (`ROUND(1234.5678, -2)` = 1200).
- Exact numbers (DECIMAL/NUMERIC/INT) round **half away from zero**: 2.5 becomes 3 and -2.5 becomes -3. SQL Server rounds FLOAT the same way.
- MySQL FLOAT/DOUBLE depend on the C library and often round half to even; keep money in DECIMAL.
- Result keeps the input scale: `ROUND(2.5, 0)` shows `3` in MySQL and `3.0` in SQL Server. Cast if the display matters.
- Round **after** you sum, not before: `ROUND(SUM(x), 2)`, otherwise rounding errors accumulate.

args.name: d (position 2)
args.meaning: Digits after the decimal point to keep. Default 0 in MySQL; required in SQL Server. Negative rounds left of the point.

args.name: function (SQL Server position 3)
args.meaning: 0 (default) = round; any non-zero value = truncate instead. See the next section.

examples.title: Positive, zero and negative digits
examples.explain_md: Half away from zero on both sides of 0; a negative `d` rounds to the left of the decimal point.
examples.mysql: SELECT ROUND(2.5, 0) AS half_up, ROUND(-2.5, 0) AS half_neg, ROUND(1234.5678, 2) AS two_dec, ROUND(1234.5678, -2) AS hundreds;
examples.tsql: SELECT ROUND(2.5, 0) AS half_up, ROUND(-2.5, 0) AS half_neg, ROUND(1234.5678, 2) AS two_dec, ROUND(1234.5678, -2) AS hundreds;

examples.title: Sales tax on orders
examples.explain_md: `amount * 0.0825` has four decimals; ROUND to cents.
examples.mysql: SELECT order_id, amount, ROUND(amount * 0.0825, 2) AS tax FROM orders WHERE order_id BETWEEN 101 AND 105 ORDER BY order_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT order_id, amount, ROUND(amount * 0.0825, 2) AS tax FROM orders WHERE order_id BETWEEN 101 AND 105 ORDER BY order_id;

sections.heading: Truncate, FLOOR, CEIL
sections.body_md:
- **Truncate** (drop digits, toward zero): MySQL `TRUNCATE(x, d)`; SQL Server `ROUND(x, d, 1)` (third argument non-zero). `TRUNCATE(-1.99, 1)` = -1.9.
- `FLOOR(x)` = largest integer <= x (toward minus infinity); `CEIL(x)` / `CEILING(x)` = smallest integer >= x. For negatives they differ from truncate: `FLOOR(-1.5)` = -2, `CEIL(-1.5)` = -1, truncate = -1.
- SQL Server only has `CEILING` (no `CEIL`); MySQL has both.
- Round up to a multiple of n: `CEIL(x / n) * n`; round down: `FLOOR(x / n) * n`. Ceiling of a division needs a decimal division (see the division section).
- Bucketing: `FLOOR(salary / 50000) * 50000` makes salary bands.

args.name: d (TRUNCATE position 2)
args.meaning: Decimals to keep; negative zeroes digits left of the point (`TRUNCATE(1999, -2)` = 1900). MySQL requires it.

args.name: 1 (ROUND position 3)
args.meaning: SQL Server: non-zero flag turns ROUND into truncate.

examples.title: Negative numbers are the trap
examples.explain_md: FLOOR goes down, CEIL goes up, truncate goes toward zero.
examples.mysql: SELECT FLOOR(-1.5) AS floor_neg, CEIL(-1.5) AS ceil_neg, TRUNCATE(-1.99, 1) AS trunc_neg, FLOOR(7.9) AS floor_pos, CEIL(7.1) AS ceil_pos, TRUNCATE(7.987, 2) AS trunc_pos;
examples.tsql: SELECT FLOOR(-1.5) AS floor_neg, CEILING(-1.5) AS ceil_neg, ROUND(-1.99, 1, 1) AS trunc_neg, FLOOR(7.9) AS floor_pos, CEILING(7.1) AS ceil_pos, ROUND(7.987, 2, 1) AS trunc_pos;

examples.title: 50k salary bands
examples.explain_md: FLOOR(salary / 50000) * 50000 gives the band start; the decimal literal keeps SQL Server from truncating early.
examples.mysql: SELECT name, salary, FLOOR(salary / 50000.0) * 50000 AS band_start FROM employees WHERE salary IS NOT NULL AND emp_id <= 5 ORDER BY emp_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT name, salary, FLOOR(salary / 50000.0) * 50000 AS band_start FROM employees WHERE salary IS NOT NULL AND emp_id <= 5 ORDER BY emp_id;

sections.heading: ABS, MOD / %, POWER, SQRT, SIGN
sections.body_md:
- `ABS(x)` absolute value. `SIGN(x)` returns -1, 0 or 1.
- Modulo: `x % y` works in both engines; `MOD(x, y)` and `x MOD y` are MySQL only. SQL Server has no MOD function.
- The remainder takes the sign of the **dividend**: `-17 % 5` = -2 and `17 % -5` = 2 (both engines).
- `x % 0`: MySQL returns NULL; SQL Server raises a divide-by-zero error.
- `POWER(x, y)` = x^y (MySQL also `POW`). Returns a float. `SQRT(x)` errors on negatives in SQL Server, returns NULL in MySQL.
- Logarithms: MySQL `LOG(x)` natural, `LOG(base, x)` two-argument with **base first**; SQL Server `LOG(x [, base])` with the base **second**. `LOG10(x)` is the same in both.
- Even/odd test: `id % 2 = 0`. Every-nth-row sampling: `id % 10 = 0`.

syntax.mysql:
MOD(n, m)  /  n % m  /  n MOD m
POWER(x, y)
SQRT(x)
LOG(base, x)
syntax.tsql:
n % m
POWER(x, y)
SQRT(x)
LOG(x, base)

args.name: m (MOD position 2)
args.meaning: Divisor; 0 gives NULL (MySQL) or an error (SQL Server).

examples.title: Modulo with signs
examples.explain_md: Remainder follows the dividend's sign. `MOD(17, 5)` and `17 % 5` agree.
examples.mysql: SELECT ABS(-7) AS abs_v, MOD(17, 5) AS mod_fn, 17 % 5 AS mod_op, -17 % 5 AS mod_neg, SIGN(-9) AS sign_v, POWER(2, 10) AS pow_v, SQRT(144) AS root_v;
examples.tsql: SELECT ABS(-7) AS abs_v, 17 % 5 AS mod_fn, 17 % 5 AS mod_op, -17 % 5 AS mod_neg, SIGN(-9) AS sign_v, POWER(2, 10) AS pow_v, SQRT(144) AS root_v;
examples.dialect_note_md: SQL Server has no `MOD()`, so both modulo columns use `%`.

examples.title: Even employee ids
examples.mysql: SELECT emp_id, name FROM employees WHERE MOD(emp_id, 2) = 0 ORDER BY emp_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT emp_id, name FROM employees WHERE emp_id % 2 = 0 ORDER BY emp_id;

sections.heading: Division: decimal vs integer
sections.body_md:
The most-tested numeric trap.
- MySQL `/` is **always decimal**: `7 / 2` = 3.5000. Integer division is the `DIV` operator: `7 DIV 2` = 3 (truncates toward zero, so `-7 DIV 2` = -3). `%` gives the remainder.
- SQL Server `/` with two integers **truncates**: `7 / 2` = 3. Make one side decimal to get 3.5: `7 * 1.0 / 2`, `7 / 2.0` or `CAST(7 AS DECIMAL(10,2)) / 2`.
- Percentages and averages are where this bites: `COUNT(*) / total` is 0 in SQL Server unless multiplied by `100.0` first.
- Ceiling of a division: `CEIL(7 / 2)` is 4 in MySQL but 3 in SQL Server (the division already truncated). Write `CEILING(7 / 2.0)` for both.
- SQL Server `AVG(int_col)` truncates too: use `AVG(col * 1.0)`.

syntax.mysql:
a / b       -- decimal
a DIV b     -- integer quotient
syntax.tsql:
a / b                -- int / int truncates
a * 1.0 / b          -- decimal result

args.name: b
args.meaning: Divisor. 0 gives NULL in MySQL SELECTs (error in strict INSERT/UPDATE) and an error in SQL Server - guard with NULLIF(b, 0).

examples.title: Force decimal division
examples.explain_md: `7 * 1.0 / 2` is 3.5 in both engines; ceiling of 7/2.0 is 4.
examples.mysql: SELECT 7 * 1.0 / 2 AS decimal_div, CEILING(7 / 2.0) AS ceil_div, 7 % 2 AS remainder;
examples.tsql: SELECT 7 * 1.0 / 2 AS decimal_div, CEILING(7 / 2.0) AS ceil_div, 7 % 2 AS remainder;

examples.title: Integer division
examples.explain_md: MySQL needs DIV for a whole-number quotient; the SQL Server `/` on two integers already truncates.
examples.mysql: SELECT 7 / 2 AS slash, 7 DIV 2 AS div_op, -7 DIV 2 AS div_negative;
examples.tsql: SELECT 7 / 2 AS slash, 7 / 2 AS div_op, -7 / 2 AS div_negative;
examples.dialect_note_md: In real SQL Server this returns 3, 3, -3 (integer division truncates). MySQL `/` returns 3.5000, `DIV` returns 3 and -3. The in-browser SQL Server emulator shows 3.5 for `7 / 2` - the same trap in reverse.

sections.heading: Percentages, ratios and safe division
sections.body_md:
Pattern: `100.0 * part / total`, then ROUND.
- Put the decimal (`100.0`) **first** so the multiplication happens before an integer division can truncate.
- Share of total: `100.0 * COUNT(*) / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM t)` or `100.0 * SUM(x) / SUM(SUM(x)) OVER ()`.
- Guard the denominator: `100.0 * part / NULLIF(total, 0)`; wrap in `COALESCE(..., 0)` if NULL is not wanted.
- Percent change: `100.0 * (new - old) / NULLIF(old, 0)`. Growth is relative to the **old** value.
- Percentage points vs percent: 10% to 12% is +2 points but +20% relative.
- Conditional share: `100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN cond THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*)`.

examples.title: Order status share
examples.explain_md: 11 of 14 orders are completed. `100.0 * COUNT(*) / (...)` stays decimal; the subquery gives the total.
examples.mysql: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS orders_n, ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders), 1) AS pct FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;
examples.tsql: SELECT status, COUNT(*) AS orders_n, ROUND(100.0 * COUNT(*) / (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders), 1) AS pct FROM orders GROUP BY status ORDER BY status;

examples.title: Year-over-year growth
examples.explain_md: Join each 2024 month to the same month a year earlier; growth is (new - old) / old.
examples.mysql: SELECT cur.month_start, cur.revenue, ROUND(100.0 * (cur.revenue - prev.revenue) / NULLIF(prev.revenue, 0), 1) AS yoy_pct FROM monthly_revenue cur JOIN monthly_revenue prev ON prev.month_start = cur.month_start - INTERVAL 1 YEAR WHERE cur.month_start < '2024-04-01' ORDER BY cur.month_start;
examples.tsql: SELECT cur.month_start, cur.revenue, ROUND(100.0 * (cur.revenue - prev.revenue) / NULLIF(prev.revenue, 0), 1) AS yoy_pct FROM monthly_revenue cur JOIN monthly_revenue prev ON prev.month_start = DATEADD(YEAR, -1, cur.month_start) WHERE cur.month_start < '2024-04-01' ORDER BY cur.month_start;

pitfalls_md: Rounded shares need not add up: three rows rounded to one decimal can total 99.9 or 100.1.
SQL Server DECIMAL division can shrink the result scale (e.g. `DECIMAL(10,2) / DECIMAL(10,2)` keeps at least 6 decimals); the result is still correct but cast to a fixed scale for display.

sections.heading: CAST and CONVERT to DECIMAL / INT / text
sections.body_md:
- `CAST(x AS type)` is ANSI and works in both engines. `CONVERT` differs: **MySQL `CONVERT(x, type)`** has the value first; **SQL Server `CONVERT(type, x [, style])`** has the type first.
- `DECIMAL(p, s)`: p = total digits, s = digits after the point. `DECIMAL(10, 2)` holds up to 99999999.99. Overflow is an error; extra decimals are rounded.
- MySQL `CAST` target types are limited: `SIGNED`/`UNSIGNED` (integers), `DECIMAL(p,s)`, `CHAR`, `DATE`, `DATETIME`, `DOUBLE`. `CAST(x AS VARCHAR(10))` and `AS INT` are **errors** in MySQL; use `CHAR` and `SIGNED`.
- SQL Server `CAST(x AS INT)` of a decimal **truncates** (12.99 becomes 12); MySQL `CAST(12.99 AS SIGNED)` **rounds** (13).
- Failed conversion of text: SQL Server errors (`TRY_CAST` / `TRY_CONVERT` return NULL); MySQL returns 0 for 'abc' with a warning, or the numeric prefix of '12abc'.

syntax.tsql:
CAST(expr AS type)
CONVERT(type, expr [, style])
TRY_CAST(expr AS type)

args.name: type
args.meaning: Target type. MySQL: SIGNED, UNSIGNED, DECIMAL(p,s), CHAR, DATE... SQL Server: any type.

args.name: CONVERT position order
args.meaning: MySQL: (value, type). SQL Server: (type, value, style).

examples.title: Text to DECIMAL, number to text
examples.explain_md: `CAST('12.345' AS DECIMAL(10,2))` rounds to 12.35. MySQL converts to text with CHAR; SQL Server uses VARCHAR.
examples.mysql: SELECT CAST('12.345' AS DECIMAL(10, 2)) AS as_decimal, CAST(7 AS CHAR) AS as_text, CONVERT('12.5', DECIMAL(5, 1)) AS convert_fn;
examples.tsql: SELECT CAST('12.345' AS DECIMAL(10, 2)) AS as_decimal, CAST(7 AS VARCHAR(10)) AS as_text, CONVERT(DECIMAL(5, 1), '12.5') AS convert_fn;

examples.title: Decimal to integer: round or truncate?
examples.explain_md: The same-looking cast gives different results.
examples.mysql: SELECT CAST(12.99 AS SIGNED) AS as_int, CAST(-12.99 AS SIGNED) AS as_int_neg;
examples.tsql: SELECT CAST(12.99 AS INT) AS as_int, CAST(-12.99 AS INT) AS as_int_neg;
examples.dialect_note_md: Real SQL Server returns 12 and -12 (truncates); MySQL returns 13 and -13 (rounds). Use `FLOOR` / `ROUND` explicitly when the intent matters.

sections.heading: GREATEST and LEAST (row-wise max/min)
sections.body_md:
- `GREATEST(a, b, c)` / `LEAST(a, b, c)` compare **values in one row**; `MAX` / `MIN` aggregate down **rows**.
- MySQL returns **NULL if any argument is NULL**. Wrap with `COALESCE` for 'ignore missing'.
- SQL Server added `GREATEST` / `LEAST` in **2022** (and Azure SQL); the documented behaviour is to ignore NULL arguments, so results differ from MySQL when a NULL is present. Before 2022 use `CASE` or `(SELECT MAX(v) FROM (VALUES (a), (b)) AS t(v))`.
- Common uses: floor a value (`GREATEST(x, 0)`), cap a value (`LEAST(x, 100000)`), latest of several date columns.

args.name: v1, v2, ...
args.meaning: Two or more values or columns from the same row; the result type follows normal precedence.

examples.title: Floor and cap
examples.explain_md: Row-wise comparison of literals; the cap keeps values under 100,000.
examples.mysql: SELECT GREATEST(3, 9, 5) AS biggest, LEAST(3, 9, 5) AS smallest, GREATEST(-4, 0) AS floored_at_zero, LEAST(150000, 100000) AS capped;
examples.tsql: SELECT GREATEST(3, 9, 5) AS biggest, LEAST(3, 9, 5) AS smallest, GREATEST(-4, 0) AS floored_at_zero, LEAST(150000, 100000) AS capped;
examples.dialect_note_md: Requires SQL Server 2022+; on older versions use CASE expressions.

examples.title: NULL arguments differ by engine
examples.explain_md: MySQL propagates NULL; SQL Server 2022 ignores it.
examples.mysql: SELECT GREATEST(3, NULL, 7) AS greatest_null, LEAST(3, NULL, 7) AS least_null;
examples.tsql: SELECT GREATEST(3, NULL, 7) AS greatest_null, LEAST(3, NULL, 7) AS least_null;
examples.dialect_note_md: MySQL returns NULL for both. SQL Server 2022 returns 7 and 3 (NULL arguments are ignored).

examples.title: Cap salaries (NULL-safe)
examples.explain_md: COALESCE first so Jon's NULL becomes 0 instead of NULL in MySQL; then LEAST caps at 100,000.
examples.mysql: SELECT name, salary, LEAST(COALESCE(salary, 0), 100000) AS capped FROM employees WHERE emp_id IN (2, 4, 8, 10) ORDER BY emp_id;
examples.tsql: SELECT name, salary, LEAST(COALESCE(salary, 0), 100000) AS capped FROM employees WHERE emp_id IN (2, 4, 8, 10) ORDER BY emp_id;
